item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This was a long one! Probably took me around… What, 40 minutes to an hour to read this? But let me tell you, it was worth it. I've been kinda putting off reading this for a while now, mostly because of how intimidating the size of it was, but I'm so glad I got around to finally read it. It's so complex and filled with great addendums and photos… It was all just so amazing. One of the greatest SCPs I've read.

Big +1 from me.

Questions
– hide block
  • "Not desire, more than it was impulse." There's some appropriately ornate language going on in this article; is there something wrong with this sentence, or is this how it was meant to read? Is it missing a "that"?
  • "…the woman's dismembered hand falls to the floor." This event was taking place outside if I'm not mistaken, so would "ground" be more appropriate than "floor"?
  • Was Bumaro aware that the heart was a forgery? (I think so.)
  • Is SCP-2399 here "The Invincible" from Final Fantasy 9? (I think so.1)
  • Is POI-004D/001 the chain-dreads woman? (I think so.)
Nitpicks
– hide block

Here are some issues that didn't affect my rating:

  • There are inconsistencies with the syntactical formatting of the footnotes with regard to punctuation. (I know this is a split hair, but I feel the need to point it out as this is an 001 proposal, and because the discrepancy occurs as closely as three sentences apart.)
  • Bumaro, while at times is an incredibly effective, manipulative, and unsavory bastard,2 also at times reads like a Saturday-morning cartoon villain ("A minor setback," "…until they are powerless to stop him."… we're only missing a diabolical cackle.)
  • There's an unnecessary compulsion effect at play in the first correspondence of Addendum 6 ("…just to throw themselves in it. Said they were shredding like jumping under a lawn-mower."), and again in Addendum 11 ("Said it looked like he'd shoved it in there himself."). I don't know what it adds except a potential irritant, given the site's general consensus on compulsions. I think this was a risky addition, but it clearly hasn't hurt the article.
  • "There's this story that gets told among Foundation agents… they still get it right…They say, 'Don't you know? The GOC killed God.'… the greenhorns will say, "No, that's not true'… Then the vets will smile and shake their heads, and won't say anything." Cool story, Hansel.3
  • The article, like the entity it describes, seems to hungrily incorporate whatever is in the immediate thematic vicinity, including GoIs and skips. Not a negative really, in fact it is a nice parallel, but it comes off as a grab-all attempt. (E.g. I think the exclusion of the UIU would have helped, as their role doesn't really come back around in any centralized way. They feel thrown in for the sake of their appearance.)
Negatives
– hide block
  • The "Been There, Shaped History" here is enjoyable, but it unfortunately has to be justified by retrofitting all maps of the area, which is a bit of a stretch that almost seems like a handwave. In the end, the unbelievability outweighs the need for and the effect of the trope, imo.
  • Philosophically, the end of the piece backs off from what makes the GoI itself, rejecting the orthodox primacy of literal mechanical parts and questioning the possibility of the God being "broken" at all, for something more pantheistic. While I appreciate this (though a wee bit cliché) the article doesn't sustain this philosophy, and quickly telescopes back to mechanical components and brokenness, which makes the whole motion a bit of a philosophical whiplash that I'm not sure makes the spiritual impact that it attempts to.
  • This is as close to an indisputably great article as you're likely to come across on the site, but I am not confident in its casting as an 001. Because of the aforementioned spiritual flop, I don't think its scope, or the entity itself, is sufficient. In addition, chronological arguments for this being 001 aren't here. I understand that 001 as chronology is an optional consideration for authors, and don't hold it against the authors direly, but the absence of any redeeming arguments to grab onto doesn't help; by the time SCP-001 amasses here, there is established Foundation leadership, other documented anomalies, rival GoIs with their own artifacts, and a mention of SCP-2399 which may or may not insinuate the existence of several thousand other anomalies.
Positives
– hide block
  • The immersion is impeccable and the atmosphere is vivid and memorable.
  • The subtlety of the article:
    • The thematic threading of repeated phrasing ("wasn't as heavy as you'd think") is masterful.
    • "Bits of the monster will work to destroy itself, deploy smaller entities to do the job." Before I read this line, I was pretty confused by the inclusion of the chain-dreads woman. This is one of the most important lines of the piece, and yet could easily be missed.
  • This is one of the few times I've seen an article find in-universe justification for the pacing of its stingily-revealed information. Instead of being a huge example of "Being as Unhelpful as Possible" for the sake of narrative effect, the Factory's involvement being tucked-away towards the end of the article is justified by the order for obfuscation (realized in the accompanying footnote, regardless of its truth), seen in the special containment procedures.
  • I respect that the authors lay out the entirety of the events in the description, giving a believable and straightforward synopsis for in-universe personnel, while successfully sustaining the interest of readers to where the rest of the (massive) article doesn't feel like repeated information.
  • The characterization of the 001 entity is just so neat. There are notes of both terror and empathy in it, and it becomes the most meaningful metaphor of the article.
  • "God is much simpler than that. God is everything." These two lines are neat together.

tl;dr: This is a great article.

Footnotes
1. Having a bit of fun here!
2. Especially if the answer to the above question about him is "yes".
3. And here!

item.content:encoded:
I love this one. It's probably my favorite 001. Big, dramatic scope without trying too hard to overwrite other ideas, and very good use of multiple SCPs and GoIs. I'm definitely not a big fan of the expanded Broken Church lore that's popped up in recent years (the Mekhane and vs Sarkic stuff), so I particularly like this story: the Church of the Broken God are a bunch of crazies just jamming different mechanical bits together in an effort to revive a god born from their own delusion or misunderstanding of reality. The pictures aren't the best photoshop in the world but even still they really add to the article.
Love it, love it, love it.

item.title: Headcanon regarding the ''Maksur'' object class and SCP-001 critique
item.content:encoded:
The ''Maksur'' object class is given to an SCP object of high importance that requires the combination of two or more SCP objects to exist. This is to be taken a grain of salt (If you want it to), but it's just something I had in mind.

Also, this has to be my favorite SCP-001 proposal mostly because it can exist alongside other SCP-001 proposals, given that you have to assemble it with previously existing SCPs. I wonder how this ties into the CoBG-Sarkic stories. Perhaps a weapon? A body for Mekhane? Only time will tell. I call dibs on a Yaldaboth SCP. -Cat hiss-

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
There are some quality pieces among the 001 proposals, but I honestly have to say, out of the lot, this is the one that most thoroughly entertained me. It evokes the essence of the SCP universe at it's most volatile, incorporating some of the better GoIs while justifying the Foundation's own existence with a spectacle that, itself, is just the tiniest glimpse of the lunacy that would ensue if their ever-so-valiant efforts were to fall short.

If you made a movie out of SCPs, this is the kind of thing that would be the climactic sequence, at which you throw most of the effects budget, with superlative enthusiasm and zero regrets.

Okay, I will be frank: I LOVE THIS!

Maybe it is because I am relatively new to the site, and haven't been grinded down by years of reused tropes and constantly shifting storylines, but gosh darn it, this is SO COOL to me!

I was expecting the broken god to just be another "if deze tings get to close, den oh teh noes, eval robit tiem, y'all", but this made it so much…. more. It wasn't just another anthropophobic creature. It was more like a cosmic Iron-Giant than a psycho Liberty Prime. That being said, it was sort of suprising that its method of suicide was to have somebody shoot it with an alien death-ray.

I also found it really cool that so many of the GOI's actually interacted with each other. It's easy to forget they all share a universe sometimes.

I could go on, but nobody likes essay-length comments.

Short version: Giant Death Robot Vs Giant Death Spaceship = upvote

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
It's a really amazing feat of writing to juggle all those GoIs and cross-references and largely succeed (although the strain does show occasionally.)

The broken-god-deism bit at the end is probably my favourite SCP meta-origin (that's what you were going for, right?); no silly attempts to go "ah, they look weird, but they're really all from the same universe/mad scientist." Maybe they're parts of something larger, but they're very small and very different parts of something very large and complicated. Also, turns out God hates cross-testing and doing it makes Him sad :D

If it was any other number, I would have upvoted. This is an objectively good SCP.

But at the end of the day: this is a giant death robot.

It's a very large giant death robot, and it was made by combining the work of several GoIs, and it ties into the larger universe, but it's still just a giant death robot.

There are lots of SCPs that killed a bunch of people, needed a huge coverup, tie into other SCPs. There are quite a few SCPs that imply much bigger things about the nature of the universe than this one. It's not particularly "foundational" or key to the Foundation's history; it's not "the most important SCP".

Why is this 001?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
You know I love the both of you, so it pains me to give this a negative vote. It's difficult to say exactly what irks me about this — I would adore it just fine as a tale, which are excellent places to synthesize a lot of existing concepts into a new pseudo-canon. But as a 001 proposal, it feels like an exercise in just how epic can we make a 001? How many disparate groups of interest, mechanical objects, can we weave together into a single narrative?

It brings these new elements in at a rapid-fire pace but gives no time to make them more than shadows on the wall, window dressing to increase the scale of the event. It's already quite long — the longest 001, perhaps? — but still doesn't give enough time to make any of its massive cast of characters, groups and concepts click as interesting on their own.

7.8/10 too much water

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The thing about SCP-001 entries: a lot of them are good, but none of them feel definitive. They feel like really well-written entries, but- with the possible exception of the Database- none of them feel like they deserve to be called SCP-001. SCP-001 needs to be something that has a powerful connection with the Foundation itself, and to other skips, but also needs to be something intimidating on its own.

The thing about the Broken God: it's scarier in pieces. The idea that these objects, many of which are quite deadly on their own, are just parts of some unimaginable whole, is something that makes the ground fall out from under you. But attempting to portray the thing itself inevitably falls short. Nothing lives up to the expectations of unimaginable mechanized horror. The whole is, somehow, less than the sum of its parts.

Both of those things were absolutes. Until I read this article.

Not only does this feel like a definitive SCP-001 proposal, but the Broken God is somehow just as horrifying- if not MORE horrifying- than we always envisioned. Needless to say, +1.
